title: Humanity Is Plagued By The Open Loop
body: We're obsessed with closing loops. Say goodbye before someone dies. Get the last word in an argument. Finish the project instead of shelving it. Get an answer, any answer, instead of sitting with "I don't know."

A lot of the time, the other side of that loop doesn't even know it's open. If someone dies before you get to say goodbye, they don't experience an incomplete goodbye. There's no ledger on their end waiting to be balanced. The open loop was always yours. You were closing something in your own head.

An open loop can be as simple as not knowing where you stand. Did I handle that? Is this going to come back on me? Not knowing is uncomfortable. An answer gives you something solid, even when the answer isn't particularly good. It's why you re-send an email you already sent or keep explaining a decision that was already fine. You're not necessarily changing the outcome. You just want to know where things stand.

Unfinished things also have a way of hanging around in your head longer than they deserve. An unanswered text isn't as important as an unfinished project, obviously. But that doesn't stop you from checking your phone six times while ignoring the project.
**Learn the art of letting things die**
The bigger problem is that plenty of these things never deserved much attention in the first place.

You have an idea and write it down. Someone says, "We should do that sometime." You think it might be nice to learn Spanish, redo the kitchen, start a podcast, read a particular book, call someone, fix something around the house. Now it exists somewhere in your head or on a list.
And because it's there, you keep treating it like something you haven't done yet.

We usually think prioritizing means figuring out what comes first. But you also have to decide what you're not going to do at all. Otherwise every idea, wish, suggestion and half-formed intention gets to hang around indefinitely.

list: If you've already decided not to do something, cross it off. Don't keep carrying it because you might change your mind someday. If it matters enough, it'll come back.
Keep a list, but don't pretend everything on it has equal standing. Pick the few things that actually matter and work on those.

Some loops belong to someone else. You may want a response, an explanation or some kind of resolution from another person and never get it. At some point, waiting for them to close it just keeps it open in your own head.

body: Not everything needs to be finished. Some things need to be finished, some need to be decided, and some need to be dropped.
